title: Hold Your Tongue, Check Your Story
sum: Ben Sira starts with the habits that ruin a young man: drink, women and a loose tongue (19:1-12). The fool cannot keep a secret: a word inside him is like a baby in labor or an arrow in the thigh. Then comes a lesson in fairness: before you act on what you heard about a friend or neighbor, take it up with him, because the story may be slander, and leave the rest to the law of the Most High (19:13-17).

The second half of the chapter sets true wisdom against mere cleverness. All wisdom is the fear of the Lord and includes doing the law (19:20). A simple person who fears God is better than a brilliant lawbreaker (19:24), and there is a shrewdness that is exact but unjust, like the scoundrel who bows in black and plots behind his mournful face (19:25-28). Yet a careful observer can read a man's character in his clothes, his laugh and his walk (19:29-30).
readings: Read as rules for a young man

The chapter is practical advice for pupils heading into public life: stay sober, keep confidences, check rumors before you act, and learn to see through hypocrites. Its wisdom is the wisdom of Proverbs applied to the city and the court.
Read as a teaching on the law

The center of the chapter is 19:17 and 19:20. Correcting a neighbor and refusing to act on hearsay are commands of Leviticus 19:17-18, the chapter that ends 'love your neighbor'. On this reading Ben Sira's manners are the law of Moses lived out in daily speech, and Jesus' rule in Matthew 18:15 stands in the same line.

views.C: In the Catholic Old Testament Sirach is Scripture, and this chapter is read as inspired moral teaching on prudence in speech and on fraternal correction, the duty Matthew 18:15 also lays down.
views.O: Orthodox Bibles read Sirach in the Greek, the base text of this page. The Greek's rule 'take it up with your friend' before believing a story fits the church's long teaching against judging and slander.
views.P: Protestants who keep the Apocrypha, such as Anglicans and Lutherans, read it for example of life, not for doctrine. The advice here on gossip and correction agrees closely with Proverbs, James 3 and Matthew 18, so it raises no conflict with the 66 books.
views.H: Historians read the chapter as the teaching of a Jerusalem scribe of the early 100s BC. The verses found only in the longer Greek (19:18-19, 21) are later additions; one of them speaks of immortality, an idea the base text does not hold.
views.J: Ben Sira was not received into the Jewish Bible, but Jews kept copying his sayings. A medieval anthology from the Cairo Genizah, MS C, preserves the Hebrew of 19:1-3, the only Hebrew that survives from this chapter.

deep.h: How much Hebrew survives for chapters 19-23
deep.b:
For most of Sirach a good part of the Hebrew is known from the Cairo Genizah manuscripts and the Masada scroll. For chapters 19-23 very little is. David Kahana's 1912 edition prints only 19:1-2, 20:5-7, 20:13 and 21:22-23, plus a saying the Talmud attributes to Ben Sira, which he places after 21:23 (see the note there). All of it comes from Genizah MS C, a medieval collection of excerpts, not a continuous copy of the book. The bensira.org transcriptions of MS C add 19:3, 20:22-23, 20:30-31, 21:26, 22:11-12, 22:21-22 and 23:11. Everywhere else in these five chapters the grandson's Greek is the oldest text there is.

Where MS C survives, the variants give its readings. It differs in interesting ways: 'one who does this' for 'a drunken worker' (19:1), a command 'do not draw a sword' for 'if you draw a sword' (22:21), 'atonement' and 'repentance' for the Greek's 'a way back' and 'reconciliation' (22:21-22).

Verses 19:18, 19:19 and 19:21 have no line in Codex Vaticanus, the base text. They belong to the longer Greek text, a revision known from later manuscripts and followed by the KJV. The site keeps every verse number so that references match other Bibles, and shows these lines in brackets, translated from codex 248 as J. H. A. Hart printed it in 1909. The Latin Vulgate does not have these three verses. The longer Greek also adds lines inside other verses (19:5, 6, 8, 17, 20, 25); each has a variant entry, because the KJV translates them.

echoes: Proverbs 23:20-21; 1 Corinthians 6:16; Leviticus 5:1; Leviticus 19:17-18; Matthew 18:15; Proverbs 14:15; James 3:2; Proverbs 1:7; Job 28:28; Matthew 6:16; 1 Samuel 16:7

settings.by: Jesus son of Sirach (Ben Sira) of Jerusalem, a teacher and scribe (50:27)
settings.to: His pupils, the young men he calls 'my child' and invites to his 'house of instruction' (51:23)
settings.when: Jerusalem, in the early 100s BC, before the crisis under Antiochus IV
settings.why: To warn pupils about the habits that ruin a career and a reputation: drunkenness, prostitutes and gossip. Knowing that the hearers were young men about to enter public life explains the stress on keeping confidences: a counselor who repeats what he hears will soon be trusted by no one.
settings.readers: The grandson's Greek readers in Egypt after he translated the book (the prologue gives the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes); later Jewish copyists, whose medieval excerpts of these sayings survive in Cairo Genizah MS C; and the rabbis, who quoted 'the book of ben Sira' (Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 16b). In the churches the Greek, and later the Latin, made the book a manual of conduct.
views: A real school
Taken at its word, 51:23 means Ben Sira taught young men who were training to serve as scribes, counselors and officials, and these chapters are lessons for them.
A literary frame
'My child' and 'house of instruction' may be the conventions of wisdom writing, as in Proverbs 1:8, and the book may have been written for any educated reader.

title: A Time to Be Silent
sum: Chapter 20 is built from short paired sayings, most beginning 'there is'. The first group is about speech and silence (20:1-8): a rebuke at the wrong time, a silence that is wise and one that only hides an empty head, a braggart who misses the moment. A second group is about gains that are losses and losses that are gains (20:9-17): gifts that pay back double and gifts that are bait, a fool whose one gift comes with many eyes watching for a return.

The last third turns again to the tongue (20:18-26): a slip on the floor is better than a slip of the tongue, a proverb in a fool's mouth is wasted, shame can make a person promise what he should not, and a habitual liar is worse than a thief. Under the heading 'Sayings in proverbs' (20:27-31), the chapter ends with advice for life near the powerful and a warning that hidden wisdom helps no one.
readings: Read as the art of timing
The key word is 'time' (20:1, 6, 7, 19, 20). Ben Sira teaches the same lesson as Ecclesiastes 3:7, 'a time to keep quiet and a time to speak': a true word at the wrong moment is still a wrong word.
Read as a warning about court life

20:27-29 show a sage who knows how the powerful work: speech wins favor, favor can smooth over a wrong, and gifts blind even the wise. Ben Sira does not praise this; he describes it so his pupils will be ready for it and not be bought.

views.C: Read as Scripture, the chapter's praise of timely speech and its condemnation of lying (20:24-26) belong with the commandment against false witness, and its warning about gifts with the law against bribes (Deuteronomy 16:19).
views.O: Orthodox spiritual writers prize silence, and readers in that tradition find in 20:5-7 the difference between a silence of emptiness and a silence of discernment.
views.P: Read for example of life, the chapter is a commentary on Proverbs 10:19 and 17:27-28 and on James 1:19, 'quick to listen, slow to speak'. Nothing in it conflicts with the 66 books.
views.H: The 'there is ...' form (Hebrew yesh) is attested in the Hebrew of MS C at 20:5-6 and 20:22-23, so it goes back to Ben Sira, not to the translator. 20:30-31 recur at 41:14-15, which may suggest that some sayings circulated on their own before the book was put together.
views.J: MS C, a Jewish anthology of Ben Sira's sayings, chose several verses from this chapter (20:5-7, 13, 22-23, 30-31), which shows which sayings later Jewish readers found worth copying.

deep.h: Silence in Ben Sira and the Bible
deep.b: Proverbs already praised silence: "Even a stubborn fool, if he stays silent, is counted as wise" (Proverbs 17:28). Ben Sira refines the point. Silence is not good in itself: one person is silent because he has nothing to say, another because he is waiting for the right moment (20:6). The fool's problem is not that he talks but that he talks at the wrong time (20:7, 19-20). Ecclesiastes gives the rule, "a time to keep quiet and a time to speak" (Ecclesiastes 3:7), and James draws the Christian lesson: the tongue is small but steers the whole person (James 3:2-6).

echoes: Ecclesiastes 3:7; Proverbs 17:27-28; Proverbs 10:19; Proverbs 26:7; Psalm 41:9; Matthew 6:2; Proverbs 12:22; Deuteronomy 16:19; Exodus 23:8; Proverbs 16:14; Matthew 5:15; Matthew 25:25

title: Run from Sin as from a Snake
sum: The chapter opens with the teacher's direct appeal: 'My child, have you sinned? Do not do it any more' (21:1). Sin is a snake that bites and a lion that kills, lawlessness a two-edged sword whose wound has no cure (21:2-3). The proud lose their wealth, the poor man's prayer goes straight to God's ears, and the smooth road of sinners ends in the pit of Hades (21:4-10).

From 21:11 Ben Sira paints a gallery of the wise and the fool. Keeping the law masters a person's thoughts, and wisdom is the fear of the Lord brought to completion (21:11). The wise man's knowledge is a flood and a spring; the fool is a cracked jar (21:13-14). Discipline is chains to the fool and jewelry to the sensible (21:19, 21). The fool laughs loudly, walks into houses uninvited and listens at doors (21:20-24). The chapter ends with two dark sayings: the ungodly man who curses Satan curses himself, and the whisperer stains his own soul (21:27-28).
readings: Read as a call to repentance

21:1-10 is a short sermon on sin: stop, pray, run. The images of snake, lion and sword make sin a living enemy, as in Genesis 4:7 and 1 Peter 5:8. Read this way the chapter sits beside the prophets' calls to turn back.
Read as a portrait of character

21:11-28 is a set of sketches. The fool is not wicked so much as unteachable and rude; the sensible person is restrained, thoughtful, polite. Ben Sira shows that wisdom is seen in manners as well as in morals.

views.C: Catholic moral teaching distinguishes sin from the inclination to sin. Readers in that tradition hear in 21:1-2 the advice to stop and to seek forgiveness, and in 21:11 the idea that obedience trains the desires.
views.O: The Orthodox ascetic tradition speaks of guarding the thoughts, and 21:11 ('masters his own thoughts') is read in that light: keeping the commandments shapes the mind as well as the body.
views.P: Protestant readers will note that 21:1 joins stopping sin with prayer for the past, not with any act that earns forgiveness, and that 21:10's 'pit of Hades' is the grave in Ben Sira, though Christian readers later heard it as the road to judgment (Matthew 7:13).
views.H: Historians note Ben Sira's view of death: Hades in 21:10 is the end of life, without the judgment after death found in Daniel 12:2 and Wisdom 3. The word 'Satan' in 21:27 is debated: the Hebrew Bible already used it for a heavenly accuser (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1), but the Hebrew word also meant any adversary (1 Kings 11:14).
views.J: The Talmud cites 'the book of ben Sira' for rules about entering another's house (Niddah 16b), close to 21:22-23, and teaches that the Torah is the antidote to the evil inclination (Kiddushin 30b), the idea behind 21:11.

deep.b: The Greek has ton satanan, the word the New Testament uses for Satan. Ben Sira's point is clear whatever the word means: a person who curses someone else for his own sin curses himself. If it is the devil, the sinner who blames the tempter is still responsible for his choice, as Ben Sira insists in 15:11-12. If it is a human adversary, the curse rebounds on the one who speaks it. The rabbis later identified Satan with the evil inclination (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 16a), and on that reading the line is almost a riddle: cursing Satan is cursing the self. The Hebrew of the verse is lost, so we cannot know whether Ben Sira wrote satan, 'adversary', or another word.

title: Fools, Daughters and Friends
sum: The chapter begins with contempt for the lazy one, a filthy stone and a lump of dung (22:1-2), and with the shame of undisciplined children (22:3-10). Ben Sira's harsh line that 'a daughter is born to his loss' (22:3) is softened by 22:4, where a sensible daughter gains a husband, but it reflects how much a daughter's honor weighed on a father. Then he turns to the fool again: teaching him is gluing broken pottery, his life is worse than death, and he is heavier to carry than sand, salt and iron (22:7-18).

The second half is about keeping friends (22:19-26). Insults drive a friend away as a stone scatters birds, but a drawn sword or angry words can be forgiven; taunting, arrogance, a betrayed secret and a stab in the back cannot. Be loyal to a friend while he is poor, and stand by him when trouble comes. The chapter ends with a prayer, 'Who will post a guard at my mouth?' (22:27), which runs into chapter 23.
readings: Read as social wisdom

Ben Sira writes for a world of family honor, where a lazy man or a shameful child disgraced the whole household, and where friendship was a bond of loyalty with duties on both sides. The chapter teaches how to protect that honor.
Read alongside the 66 books

On fools and friends the chapter echoes Proverbs closely (Proverbs 27:3; 25:9; 27:6). On daughters it goes beyond Proverbs, which praises the woman of strength (Proverbs 31:10-31), and the canon note at 22:3 sets the two side by side.

views.C: Read as Scripture, the chapter's teaching on friendship and loyalty is often valued; its words on daughters are read in context, as the advice of a father in an honor culture, not as a judgment on the dignity of women.
views.O: Orthodox readers, who read the Greek, have the same text as this page. Its friendship sayings (22:19-26) stand beside the long friendship passage of 6:5-17.
views.P: For Protestants who read the Apocrypha only for example of life, 22:3 is one of the places where Ben Sira's culture shows and where his book is weighed against the 66 books, which call children an inheritance from the LORD (Psalm 127:3).
views.H: Historians read 22:3-5 with 42:9-14 as evidence of the pressures on families in Hellenistic Jerusalem: marriage and a daughter's chastity were matters of family honor. The lines 22:9-10, found only in the longer Greek, use Greek ideas of noble and low birth.
views.J: The Hebrew of MS C survives for 22:11-12 and 22:21-22. Its 'do not draw a sword' and 'there is atonement' (22:21) give the friendship saying a different turn from the Greek.

deep.b:
Ben Sira speaks of daughters more harshly than any book of the 66. He calls a daughter 'born to his loss' (22:3), tells fathers to guard her closely (7:24; 26:10) and describes her as a hidden cause of sleeplessness (42:9-11). Yet he also says a sensible daughter wins a husband (22:4), tells fathers to see their daughters well married (7:25), and praises a good wife warmly (26:1-4, 13-18). His fears are those of his society: a daughter's chastity and marriage decided the honor of her family.

The Bible as a whole sets other notes beside these. Daughters inherit in the law (Numbers 27:8) and in Job (Job 42:15), the woman of strength is praised (Proverbs 31:10-31), and children are 'an inheritance the LORD gives' (Psalm 127:3). In the New Testament women are among Jesus' disciples and Paul's co-workers. Readers who hold Sirach as Scripture read these verses as the counsel of one father in one culture; readers who do not hold it as Scripture see here one reason to keep it below the 66.

Ben Sira draws a sharp line between a quarrel and a betrayal (22:21-22). Even a drawn sword or harsh words leave a way back. What destroys friendship is contempt, arrogance, a secret told and a treacherous blow: acts that show the friend was never trusted. He repeats the point at 27:16-21. Proverbs says the same in its own way: "Wounds from someone who loves you are true" (Proverbs 27:6). The Hebrew of MS C even gives the reason for hope: 'there is atonement', 'there is repentance' (22:21-22).

settings.what: A prayer for guarded lips and a pure heart
settings.by: Jesus son of Sirach (Ben Sira) of Jerusalem, a teacher and scribe (50:27)
settings.to: God, prayed in the hearing of his pupils as a pattern for their own prayer
settings.when: Jerusalem, in the early 100s BC, before the crisis under Antiochus IV
settings.why: To show pupils that self-control is finally a gift to pray for, not only a skill to learn. The teacher prays in the first person, asking God as Father to guard his mouth (22:27-23:1) and his desires (23:4-6), and in doing so he previews the two lessons that follow (23:7-15 and 23:16-27).
settings.readers: The grandson's Greek readers in Egypt after he translated the book (the prologue gives the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes); later Jewish copyists, whose medieval excerpts of these sayings survive in Cairo Genizah MS C; and the rabbis, who quoted 'the book of ben Sira' (Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 16b). In the churches the Greek, and later the Latin, made the book a manual of conduct.

title: Guard the Mouth and the Marriage Bed
sum: The prayer begun in 22:27 continues: 'Lord, Father and Master of my life', let whips and discipline keep watch over my thoughts so that my sins will not multiply; 'Lord, Father and God of my life', keep proud eyes, desire and lust from me (23:1-6). Then, under the title 'Discipline for the mouth', Ben Sira teaches against swearing oaths by habit and naming God carelessly, against speech 'wrapped in death', against crude talk and insults (23:7-15).

The last section is about sexual sin (23:16-27). A man burning with lust will not stop until he is consumed. The adulterer thinks the dark hides him and says, 'Who sees me?', but the eyes of the Lord are ten thousand times brighter than the sun and knew all things before they were made (23:18-20). He will be punished in public, and so will the unfaithful wife, who has broken God's law, wronged her husband and given him another man's children (23:21-26). Those who are left learn that nothing is better than the fear of the Lord (23:27).
readings: Read as a prayer and two lessons

The prayer of 22:27-23:6 asks first for a guard on the mouth, then for freedom from desire. The two lessons that follow take up the same two subjects in the same order: speech (23:7-15) and sexual sin (23:16-27). Prayer comes before instruction.
Read as teaching on God who sees

The center of the chapter is 23:19-20: nothing is hidden from God. Swearing carelessly by his name and sinning in the dark both forget that God is present. The fear of the Lord in 23:27 is the remedy for both.

views.C: Read as Scripture, 23:1 and 23:4 are among the Old Testament prayers that address God as Father. The teaching on oaths (23:9-11) and on adultery (23:16-27) fits the second and sixth commandments as the Catholic Church numbers them.
views.O: Orthodox readers hear in 23:1-6 the prayer for watchfulness over thoughts and senses that their spiritual tradition values, and they read the Greek of this page.
views.P: For Protestants who read the Apocrypha for example of life, the chapter's prayer and its warnings against careless oaths and adultery agree with the 66 books. Its words on the adulteress's children (23:24-25) are weighed against Ezekiel 18:20.
views.H: Historians note that 23:21-24 describe public punishment and a hearing before the assembly, without naming the death penalty the law of Moses prescribes (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). Whether Jewish courts of the early 100s BC carried it out is not known from this passage.
views.J: The Hebrew of MS C survives only for 23:11, on the man of many oaths. Jewish law later developed detailed rules on oaths and on avoiding the divine name, which 23:9-10 already reflect.

deep.b:
Ben Sira treats adultery as a sin of both partners. The man who 'strays from his own bed' (23:18-21) and the wife who 'deserts her husband' (23:22-26) are both punished, and both forget that God sees. The law also condemned both (Leviticus 20:10). But Ben Sira gives the woman's case more room, because of what it does to the family: an heir who is not the husband's son. His words on her children (23:24-25) are hard; they describe the shame such children met, and the note at 23:25 sets them beside Ezekiel 18:20.

Jesus later took the matter further in two directions: he counted the lustful look as adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:27-28), and when a woman caught in adultery was brought before a crowd, he would not condemn her and told her not to keep on sinning (John 8:3-11).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the prayer plans the lessons
deep.b: The prayer of 22:27-23:6 is not a stray piece placed between instructions. Its two halves match the two lessons that follow, in the same order. The first half (22:27-23:3) asks for a guard on the mouth and a seal on the lips; the lesson 'Discipline for the mouth' (23:7-15) follows. The second half (23:4-6) asks God to keep desire, gluttony and lust away; the lesson on sexual sin (23:16-27) follows. Each half opens with the same address, 'Lord, Father and ... of my life'. Read this way, Ben Sira teaches by example: he prays for what he is about to teach. This is Claude's reading of the structure, offered as an observation on the text, not as something a named scholar is reported to have said.

deep.title: Claude's theory: echoes of the Lord's Prayer
deep.b: Ben Sira's prayer has points in common with the prayer Jesus taught: the address 'Father' (23:1, 4; Matthew 6:9), the plea not to fall (23:1, 'do not let them make me fall'; Matthew 6:13, 'do not bring us into testing'), concern for sins (23:2-3; Matthew 6:12) and the enemy who would gloat (23:3; Matthew 6:13, 'the evil one'). The likeness does not show that Jesus drew on Sirach; both may simply reflect the Jewish prayer language of their times. It does show that addressing God as a personal Father in prayer had roots in Jewish piety before the Gospels.

echoes: Psalm 141:3; Isaiah 63:16; Matthew 6:9-13; Hebrews 9:7; Proverbs 6:17; Exodus 20:7; Matthew 5:34; James 5:12; Acts 22:24; Leviticus 24:16; Jeremiah 20:14; Proverbs 30:15; Proverbs 9:17; Job 24:15; Isaiah 29:15; Proverbs 15:3; Hebrews 4:13; Leviticus 20:10; John 8:3-11; Wisdom 3:16; Ezekiel 18:20; Proverbs 6:33; Psalm 19:10

settings.by: Jesus son of Sirach (Ben Sira) of Jerusalem, a teacher and scribe (50:27)
settings.to: His pupils, the young men he calls 'my child' and invites to his 'house of instruction' (51:23)
settings.when: Jerusalem, in the early 100s BC, before the crisis under Antiochus IV
settings.why: To break pupils of the habits of careless swearing, misuse of God's name, crude talk and insults, before those habits shame them in high company (23:14).
settings.readers: The grandson's Greek readers in Egypt after he translated the book (the prologue gives the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes); later Jewish copyists, whose medieval excerpts of these sayings survive in Cairo Genizah MS C; and the rabbis, who quoted 'the book of ben Sira' (Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 16b). In the churches the Greek, and later the Latin, made the book a manual of conduct.
views: A real school
Taken at its word, 51:23 means Ben Sira taught young men who were training to serve as scribes, counselors and officials, and these chapters are lessons for them.
A literary frame
'My child' and 'house of instruction' may be the conventions of wisdom writing, as in Proverbs 1:8, and the book may have been written for any educated reader.

settings.by: Jesus son of Sirach (Ben Sira) of Jerusalem, a teacher and scribe (50:27)
settings.to: His pupils, the young men he calls 'my child' and invites to his 'house of instruction' (51:23)
settings.when: Jerusalem, in the early 100s BC, before the crisis under Antiochus IV
settings.why: To warn young men, who would marry and head households, that lust is a fire that consumes, that God sees what is done in the dark, and that adultery wrecks a family's line and name. The equal warning to the adulterous wife reminded them what was at stake in their own marriages.
